en: Preface to the *Dharma-xue-mai-lun* (Treatise on the Lineage of the Dharma), composed by Ren Zhe, Court Gentleman with Rank of Tongfenglang, Acting Military Commissioner of Jianchang Commandery, and Recipient of the Scarlet Fish-Pouch.
The original mind of all people is fully endowed with Buddha-nature. Surveying broadly the various Chan teachings and all the scriptural texts, if one traces their origins...
Regarding the principle of ultimate truth, there has never been one who did not say that the true Buddha is inherently present within one's own nature.

When Bodhidharma came from the West, he pointed directly to the human mind, teaching that by seeing one's nature, one becomes a Buddha; this was because he held that one's own true Buddha does not transcend the single nature.
Everyone fails to trust themselves and thus rushes outward in search [of truth], imagining that apart from the true Buddha of one's own nature, there exists some other Buddha.
Therefore, all Buddhas and patriarchs teach the Dharma to lead people to realize the true Buddha of their own original nature, which requires no external seeking.
Furthermore, because various dharma-teachings are so profuse and manifold, they only serve to further confuse the student.

The nature of delusion has no point of entry for awakening; there is only the *Dharma-pul-kye-ron* (Treatise on the Bloodline of the Dharma) and the *Hwangbok jeon-sim-bop yo* (Essentials of the Mind-Dharma Transmission of Huangbo).
These two works are the most ultimate teachings, capable of allowing one to directly realize one's own Buddha-nature and making it easy for others to understand.

Compared to these, seeking teachers, visiting paths, poring over old scrolls, sitting in meditation, or wandering as a pilgrim are merely a wild waste of effort—the difference between them is ten thousandfold.
Twofold. This is no small contribution. Preface by Ren Zhe, the Elder Who Sees Alone, in the Guiyou year of the Shaoxing era.
The *Treatise on the Bloodline of Master Bodhidharma* states:
"The three realms arise together and all return to the One Mind. Buddhas of the past and future transmit mind-to-mind, not establishing written words."
Question: If one does not establish words and letters, what constitutes the mind? Answer: Your very question to me is your own mind;
my answer to you is my own mind. If I were without mind, by what means could I provide an answer to you? And if you were without mind, [how could you ask?]

For what reason do you ask me? To ask me is precisely your own mind. From beginningless, vast kalpas past, through all times and in all places, including every movement and activity, this is always your original mind; it is always your original Buddha.
That "the mind itself is the Buddha" is also like this. Apart from this mind, there is ultimately no other Buddha to be found.
It is so. Apart from this mind, to seek for bodhi and nirvāṇa is impossible. The reality of self-nature, the dharma that is neither cause nor effect—this is the meaning of "mind.
One's own mind is nirvāṇa. If one says that there is a Buddha or bodhi to be attained outside the mind, it is impossible.
Where, then, do the Buddha and bodhi reside? It is, for example, as if a person were to...
Can one grasp empty space with their hands? Empty space exists only as a name; it has no form or appearance.

It cannot be taken up, nor can it be discarded. This is what is meant by "being unable to seize the void. Apart from this mind, you will never see the Buddha. The Buddha is produced by one's own mind.
Why then do you seek the Buddha outside of this mind? Buddhas of the past and future have spoken only of the mind. The mind is...

This is the Buddha. The Buddha is precisely the mind. Outside the mind there is no Buddha; outside the Buddha there is no mind. If one says that the Buddha exists outside the mind, where would the Buddha be?
Since there is no Buddha outside the mind, why give rise to the perception of a Buddha? Thus, you deceive and delude one another, failing to realize your original mind.
You are seized by insentient things and lack freedom. If you do not believe this, you deceive yourself to no avail. The Buddha.

There is no fault or affliction. Sentient beings are inverted; they do not awaken to or know that their own mind is the Buddha. If one knows that one’s own mind is the Buddha, one should not seek the Buddha outside of the mind.
The Buddha does not deliver the Buddha. To seek the Buddha by means of the mind is to fail to recognize that the Buddha is nothing other than what is external.
Those who seek the Buddha in this way all fail to recognize that their own mind is the Buddha. Furthermore, one must not use the Buddha to worship the Buddha. It is not so.
One may take up the mind to recite the Buddha’s name. The Buddha does not recite sutras; the Buddha does not uphold precepts; the Buddha does not violate precepts;
the Buddha has neither upholding nor violating; nor does he create good or evil. If you wish to seek the Buddha, you must realize your nature. To realize one's nature is itself the Buddha.

If you do not realize your nature, then even reciting the Buddha’s name, chanting sutras, observing fasts, and upholding precepts will be of no benefit. By reciting the Buddha’s name, one attains cause and effect.
Reciting the sutras brings clarity of mind; upholding the precepts leads to rebirth in the heavens; practicing generosity yields karmic rewards. Yet, one will never find the Buddha by seeking him.
If you yourself do not understand clearly, you must consult a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) to realize the root of birth and death.
If you have not seen your nature, you cannot be called a spiritual friend. If it is otherwise, even if you can recite the twelve divisions of the scriptures, it is still of no avail.
One cannot avoid the cycle of birth and death; one will suffer within the three realms with no time of escape.
In the past, there was the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra, who could recite the twelve divisions of the scriptures, yet he still could not avoid the conditions of saṃsāra because he had not seen his true nature.

If even Sunakṣatra was like this, then those people of today who consider themselves followers of the Buddha-Dharma simply because they can lecture on three or five volumes of sutras and śāstras are fools.
If you do not recognize your own mind, even if you can recite secular texts and writings, they are entirely useless.
If you wish to seek the Buddha, you must directly see your nature; nature is itself the Buddha, and the Buddha is the person of freedom, the person beyond affairs and action.

If you do not see your nature, you will spend your days in a state of confusion, rushing outward in search of the Buddha, yet ultimately failing to find him. Although there is originally nothing at all, [the Buddha is right here].

It can be attained. If you seek this realization, you must also associate with virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra) and earnestly strive to bring about a deep understanding that the matter of birth and death is of great importance;

do not let it pass in vain, for self-deception is of no benefit. Even if you possess treasures as vast as mountains and a retinue as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—though these are visible when you open your eyes, are they still seen when you close them? Therefore, know that conditioned phenomena are like a dream.
Regarding illusions and the like: if one does not urgently seek out a teacher, one's entire life will pass in vain. Nevertheless, the Buddha-nature exists inherently;

yet, without relying on a teacher, it will never be clearly understood. Those who attain awakening without depending on a teacher are rare among ten thousand. If one relies solely on one's own conditions to meet [the truth], [it is exceedingly difficult].
If one attains the intent of the Sages, there is no need to consult a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra); this is the superior learning of "knowing by birth.

If one has not yet attained awakening and understanding, one must diligently and painfully engage in study; it is only through the teachings that awakening can be attained. If one has not yet fully awakened...

One may also attain it without study. This is not like the deluded who cannot distinguish black from white, falsely claiming to proclaim the Buddha’s edicts, slandering the Buddha, and showing malice toward the Dharma.
Even if such types preach the Dharma as profusely as rain, it is entirely the teaching of Māra and is certainly not the teaching of the Buddha.
Their teacher is the King of Māras, and their disciples are the subjects of Māra. Deluded people follow their directions at will, unaware that they are falling into the sea of birth and death.
However, those who have not seen their nature falsely claim to be Buddhas. Such sentient beings are great sinners; they deceive all other sentient beings and cause people to enter the realm of Māra.
If one has not seen their nature, even if they can expound the teachings of the twelve divisions of the scriptures, it is all the teaching of Māra;
they belong to the family of Māra and are not disciples of the Buddha. Since they cannot distinguish black from white, on what basis [can they be trusted]?
One is exempted from birth and death. If one sees one's nature, that is the Buddha; if one does not see one's nature, that is a sentient being.
If there were a Buddha-nature to be attained apart from the nature of sentient beings, where would the Buddha be now? Thus, the nature of sentient beings is itself the Buddha-nature.
Outside of this nature there is no Buddha; the Buddha is precisely this nature. Apart from this nature, no Buddha can be found. Outside of the Buddha...
No intrinsic nature can be apprehended.

A question is asked: "If one does not perceive this nature, what is the purpose of recollecting the Buddha, chanting the sutras, practicing generosity, observing the precepts, and exerting diligence to extensively cultivate merit and benefit?"
"Can one attain Buddhahood? He replied, "No. Again he asked, "For what reason can one not? He replied, "If there is even the slightest dharma that can be attained, this is a conditioned dharma;
it is cause and effect; it is the receiving of retribution; it is a dharma of saṃsāra. One cannot escape birth and death.

When, then, could one attain the Way of the Buddha? To become a Buddha, one must realize one's nature. If one does not realize one's nature, then talk of cause and effect and the like is merely [delusion]."

Regarding the teachings of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*): if one were to practice the teachings of the non-Buddhists, the Buddha would not be one who has transcended karma, nor would he be beyond cause and effect;
there would merely be some small dharma to be attained, all of which would be peripheral to the Buddha. By what means could [enlightenment] be accomplished?

The Buddha does not permit even a single point of attachment, a single capacity, a single understanding, or a single view. The Buddha is without transgression or observance; the nature of the mind is fundamentally empty, and it is neither defiled nor pure.

All dharmas are pure; there is neither cultivation nor realization, neither cause nor fruit. The Buddha does not uphold precepts; the Buddha does not cultivate goodness; the Buddha does not commit evil;
the Buddha does not exert diligence; the Buddha is not indolent. The Buddha is a person of non-action.

However, if one possesses a mind of attachment, even seeing the Buddha is not permitted. The Buddha is not a "Buddha"; do not interpret him as being a Buddha. If you do not perceive this meaning, [you have not seen the Buddha].
At all times and in all places, this is entirely due to not understanding one's own original mind.
If you do not see your nature, then at all times, to intend to practice the "unconditioned" (wu zuo) is to be a great sinner and a fool;

you will fall into the void of the indeterminate (wujì), as dark as a drunken man, unable to distinguish between good and evil. If you intend to cultivate the unconditioned method, you must first see your nature, and only then...
If one quiets discursive thoughts but does not perceive one's nature, it is impossible for them to attain the Buddha-way.
There are those who deny cause and effect, zealously committing evil deeds while falsely claiming that all is originally empty and thus committing evil carries no fault.
Such people fall into the dark Avīci Hell with no prospect of escape. A person of wisdom should not hold such views.
Question: Since the act of giving is a movement of the mind, and at all times it is the fundamental mind, why is this fundamental mind not perceived at the time when the physical body is impermanent?
Answer: The fundamental mind is constantly manifest; you simply do not see it.
Question: Since the mind is presently existing, why is it not seen? The Master said: Have you ever dreamed? Answer: I have dreamed. Question:
When you were dreaming, was that your own body? Answer: It was my own body. Question again:
Were your speech, activities, and movements different from yours [while awake]? Answer: They were not different. The Master said:
Since there is no distinction, this very body is your original Dharma-body; this very Dharma-body is your original mind.
This mind, from beginningless and vast kalpas until now, has not differed from what it is today. It has never undergone birth and death;
it is neither born nor extinguished, neither increasing nor decreasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither good nor evil, and neither coming nor going. Furthermore—
There is neither right nor wrong. There are no marks of male or female. There is no distinction between monastic and lay, old and young.
There is neither sage nor ordinary person. There is neither Buddha nor sentient being. There is neither cultivation nor realization. There is neither cause nor effect.

There is neither physical strength nor outward appearance. It is like empty space: it cannot be grasped, nor can it be discarded. Mountains, rivers, rocks, and walls cannot obstruct it. It transcends.
Without coming or going, with sovereign spiritual powers, one penetrates the mountain of the five aggregates and crosses the river of birth and death.
All karma is bound within this *dharmakāya*. Without attaining this mind, it is subtle and difficult to see; this mind is not the same as the mind of form. All people desire to see this mind.
Within this radiance, those who move their hands and feet are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. And when...
When questioned, they are all unable to speak; they are just like wooden puppets. This is entirely one's own experience, so why do they not recognize it?
The Buddha said: "All sentient beings are utterly deluded people. Because of this, they create karma and fall into the river of birth and death."
One attempts to emerge but sinks back down, solely because one has not seen one's nature. If sentient beings were not deluded, why would they fail to understand the matter when questioned about it?
Not a single person has been able to comprehend it. One moves one’s own hands and feet; why then is one unaware of them?

Thus we know that the words of the Sages are not mistaken; it is only the deluded who do not understand them themselves. Therefore, we know this is difficult to clarify; only the Buddha alone [can do so].
One who is able to realize this Dharma is not clearly understood by other humans, devas, or sentient beings.

If one’s wisdom is clear and lucid, this mind is termed *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), and it is also called liberation from birth and death. It is not constrained by any phenomena, nor can others constrain it;
this is named the Tathāgata, the Great Sovereign King. It is also called the Inconceivable, and it is also called the Holy Body (*āryakāya*). It is also called...
Eternal life and immortality is also called the Great Immortal (*mahā-ṛṣi*). Although the names differ, their essence is one and the same.
The various distinctions made by the sages do not depart from the self-mind. The measure of the mind is vast and its applications are inexhaustible:

it responds to the eyes seeing forms, the ears hearing sounds, the nose smelling fragrances, and the tongue discerning flavors; even down to all acts of giving and movement, these are all [the functions of] the self-mind.
The mind: at all times, that which is simply the severance of the path of language is one's own mind;
therefore it is said, "The form of the Tathāgata is inexhaustible, and wisdom is likewise so. That form is inexhaustible is one's own mind;

the mental consciousness is well able to discern all things, even down to its activities and applications—all of these are wisdom. The mind has no form or characteristics, and wisdom is likewise inexhaustible.
Therefore it is said: "The Tathāgata’s form is inexhaustible; his wisdom is likewise so. The physical body composed of the four great elements is itself the body of afflictions;
it possesses arising and ceasing. The Dharma-body is eternally abiding and has no place of dwelling. The Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is constant and never undergoes change. Thus the Sūtra says:
"Sentient beings should know that Buddha-nature is inherently possessed from the beginning. Kāśyapa simply awakened to this.
The fundamental nature (*prakṛti*). This fundamental nature is precisely the mind; the mind is precisely the nature. This nature is identical to the minds of all Buddhas.

From the Buddhas of the past to the Buddhas of the future, they transmit only this mind. Apart from this mind, no Buddha can be found. Deluded sentient beings do not know that their own mind is the Buddha;
they rush outward in pursuit, busily occupied all day long. They recite the Buddha’s name and prostrate to the Buddha, yet where is the Buddha?
One should not hold such views as these. One should simply know that within one's own mind, there is nothing else and nothing beyond it.
As the Sūtra says: "All marks whatsoever are empty and false. And again: "Wherever one is, that is where the Buddha is; one's own mind is the Buddha.
One should not use a Buddha to worship a Buddha; rather, it is when the forms and appearances of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas suddenly appear before one."
Do not at all pay homage with a mind of self-conceit. Emptiness and stillness are fundamentally non-existent;

such is their appearance. If one grasps at appearances, that is Mara; one will fall entirely into deviant paths. If this illusion arises from the mind, then there is no need for homage. Those who pay homage do not understand;

those who understand do not pay homage. Paying homage is being seized by Mara. Fearing that practitioners may not know this, I have made this distinction. Thus it is said of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas:
Within the essence of the fundamental nature, there are no such appearances whatsoever. You must take this to heart.
Should any divergent objects arise, do not attempt to grasp or analyze them, nor should you feel fear or dread; do not harbor any doubts. My mind is originally pure;
where could there be such appearances? This includes even the forms of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, ghosts and spirits, Śakra, and Brahmā.
Furthermore, do not give rise to a mind of reverence, nor be afraid. My mind is fundamentally empty and quiescent;

all appearances are merely illusory signs. Simply do not grasp at these signs. If you give rise to views of a Buddha or Dharma, or perceive the forms of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the like, and thereby produce reverence, you will fall of your own accord into the rank of ordinary beings. If you wish to directly realize [the truth], simply do not grasp at anything whatsoever.
All marks are immediately attained; there are no other words. Thus the Sūtra says: "Whatever has marks is entirely false and illusory; it possesses no fixed reality.
These illusions have no fixed characteristics and are impermanent dharmas. However, by not grasping at marks, one accords with the intention of the sages.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "To be free from all marks is itself called being a Buddha."
Question: For what reason should one not prostrate to Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others? Answer:

The celestial Māra Pāpīyān and the asuras manifest supernatural powers, all assuming the appearance of Bodhisattvas and performing various transformations; these are heterodox practitioners and are certainly not Buddhas.
The Buddha is one's own mind; do not err in your prostrations. "Buddha" is a term from the Western lands; in this land, it is called "Awakened Nature" (Juexing).

Awakening is spiritual awareness. Whether raising an eyebrow, blinking an eye, moving a hand, or shifting a foot in response to circumstances and engaging with others—all these are the nature of one's own spiritual awareness.
This nature is the mind; the mind is the Buddha; the Buddha is the Way; and the Way is Chan.

The single character "Chan" (Dhyāna) cannot be fathomed by either ordinary beings or sages. It is further said: "To see one's original nature is Chan; if one does not see one's original nature, it is not Chan.
Even if one were able to expound upon thousands of sutras and ten thousand treatises, if one does not see one's original nature, one remains a mere ordinary person;
this is not the Buddha-dharma. The Ultimate Way is profound and deep; it cannot be grasped through conversation or the scriptural teachings. By what means could one possibly reach it?
If one merely perceives the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*), even without recognizing a single character, one likewise attains the vision of nature;
this is precisely the sacred body of the Buddha. It is primordially pure, devoid of all defilement. All speech is the activity arising from the mind of a sage;

yet the essence of that activity is primordially empty, such that even names and words cannot reach it. Upon what, then, could the twelve divisions of the scriptures rely to reach it? The Way is fundamentally perfected and complete. It is not...
Through cultivation and realization, one understands that the Way transcends sound and form; it is subtle and difficult to perceive. It is like a person drinking water:

whether it is cold or warm, they know it for themselves and cannot describe it to others. Only the Tathāgata can truly know it; all other beings, such as humans and devas, remain entirely unaware of it.

The wisdom of ordinary beings does not reach this; therefore, they cling to signs. Failing to realize that their own minds are fundamentally empty and quiescent, they falsely grasp at signs and all phenomena, thereby falling into the ways of external paths. If one knows that all phenomena arise from the mind, one should have no such clinging.
If you cling to them, you will not know. If you see the original nature, the twelve divisions of the scriptures are all merely idle words;
the thousands of sutras and myriad treatises are nothing but the illumination of the mind. If you attain realization beneath a single word, what further use would the teachings have?

The ultimate truth transcends speech; the teachings are but verbal expressions and are certainly not the Way itself. The Way is fundamentally without words; words and explanations are delusions. It is like seeing palaces and towers in a dream at night.

Regarding palaces, elephants, horses, and the like, as well as trees, groves, ponds, and pavilions—regarding such appearances, one must not give rise to even a single thought of attachment or delight.
These are all places where one might be reborn; you must be most vigilant regarding this. At the time of death, do not grasp at signs, and you will immediately eliminate obstacles.
If a doubt should momentarily arise, you will be seized by Māra. The Dharmakāya is fundamentally pure and without reception.
It is solely because of delusion that one is neither aware nor knows; for this reason, one falsely undergoes retribution, whereby there is attachment to pleasure and a lack of self-mastery.
If, at this very moment, one awakens to the original body and mind, one will not be defiled by habitual tendencies.

If one proceeds from the state of a sage to that of an ordinary person, manifesting various diverse forms for the sake of sentient beings, then the sage attains mastery over both the contrary and the conformable.
All karma cannot entangle them; as noble ones who have long attained great majestic power, all categories of karma are transformed by these sages.
Neither heaven nor hell can prevail against them. The consciousness of ordinary beings is clouded and obscure, unlike that of the sages, whose inner and outer realms are transparently clear.
If one harbors doubt, one will not act; if one acts while doubting, one will drift through birth and death and later regret it.
There is no place for rescue from the signless. Poverty and suffering all arise from deluded thoughts.

If one understands this mind and encourages one another, acting without acting, one immediately enters the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision. For those who have first resolved their minds, the consciousness is entirely unsettled;
if they frequently see strange visions in dreams, they should not doubt them at all, for these all arise from one's own mind and do not come from elsewhere.
Externally, if in a dream one sees the appearance of a radiance surpassing that of the sun’s orb, then residual habits are suddenly exhausted and the nature of the Dharma-realm is perceived.
If this occurs, it is the cause for attaining the Way; one knows it only within oneself and must not speak of it to others.
Whether in a quiet garden or grove, while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one may see light—whether large or small.

Do not speak of this to others, nor should you grasp it; this too is the natural radiance of one's own nature. Or, in the stillness of night amidst darkness, while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
If you see light with your eyes such that it is no different from daylight, do not be surprised; this is simply your own mind desiring clarity.
Or, if in a night dream you see the stars and moon clearly, this is likewise your own mind’s various conditions seeking to subside. You must not speak of these things to others.
If dreams are hazy and obscure, as if walking in deep darkness, this is because the afflictive hindrances of one's own mind are heavy;

one knows this for oneself. If you perceive the original nature, there is no need for reading sutras or reciting the Buddha’s name; extensive study and vast knowledge are of no benefit, as they only cause the consciousness to become increasingly clouded.

The establishment of teachings is solely for the purpose of pointing toward the mind. If you recognize the mind, what use is there for looking at the teachings? If one proceeds from the state of an ordinary person to enter the state of a sage, then—

One must cease worldly activities to nourish the spirit and pass the days according to one's lot. If one harbors much anger and resentment, it will cause one’s nature to become increasingly contrary to the Way;
this is self-deception and of no benefit. Within the cycle of birth and death, the Sage enters and emerges with sovereign ease, appearing and disappearing without fixed pattern.
All karmic forces cannot constrain the Sage. The Sage destroys malevolent spirits and demons; all sentient beings merely perceive their original nature, while residual habits remain.

It is extinguished all at once; the spiritual consciousness is not obscured. You must realize it directly and immediately; it resides only in the present moment. If you wish to truly understand the Way, do not cling to any phenomena.

Cease karmic activity and nourish the spirit, and your residual habits will also be exhausted. Thus, clarity comes naturally without the need for strenuous effort. Non-Buddhists fail to understand the Buddha’s intent;
though they expend the most effort, they contravene the Sage’s meaning and spend their days in a frantic pursuit of thoughts.

The Buddha turned the wheel of the Dharma because people were deluded regarding their spiritual nature and could not escape saṃsāra. The Buddha was a man of leisure; why did he exhaust himself in the extensive pursuit of fame and profit?
Of what use are these things in the end? It is only for those who have not yet seen their own nature that one must read the sutras, recite the Buddha’s name, and study with constant diligence.

Practicing the Way during the six periods of the day, sitting upright without lying down, and extensively studying and accumulating much learning—regarding these as the Buddha-dharma—such sentient beings are all slanderers of the Buddha-dharma.
From the Buddhas of the past to the Buddhas of the future, it has been said only that one must see one's nature. All conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
if one does not see one's nature, to falsely claim "I have attained Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi" is a great sin. [Even those who enter] among the ten great disciples... [are included].

Among those who find it difficult to attain extensive learning, one may achieve the foremost rank; yet such a person lacks true recognition of the Buddha, studying only for the sake of erudition. Both followers of the Two Vehicles and non-Buddhists likewise lack recognition of the Buddha.

To recognize only the numerical categories of cultivation and realization is to fall within the realm of cause and effect; this is the karmic retribution of sentient beings, from which they cannot escape birth and death.
This is to turn one's back on the Buddha’s intent and is equivalent to slandering the Buddha—a being who commits no offense by killing. As the Sūtra says: "The icchantika..."
If a person does not give rise to faith, they commit no fault by killing. If one possesses faith, that person is already at the stage of a Buddha.
If you have not yet seen your nature, do not recklessly slander the virtuous; it will only deceive yourself to no avail. Good and evil are clearly manifest; cause and effect are distinct.
Heaven and hell lie right before one's eyes. The foolish who do not believe fall into the dark realms in this very life.
Within the dark hells, they neither perceive nor know [the truth], solely because their karma is so heavy that they do not believe.
It is like a blind person who does not believe there is light on the road; even if one were to speak to them of it, they would still not believe, for they are simply blind.
By what means can one distinguish the sunlight? The foolish person is likewise so:

now fallen among the various classes of animals, born into poverty and lowliness, they cannot seek life and cannot seek death. Though they undergo such suffering, when directly questioned, [they do not know].
They also say, "I am now happy; it is no different from heaven. Thus we know that all sentient beings regard their place of birth as happiness, yet they neither perceive nor understand this.
Such evil persons, solely because their karmic obstructions are heavy, are unable to give rise to faith;
this is not a matter of free will. If one sees that one's own mind is the Buddha, it does not depend on shaving off one's hair and beard.
A layperson (*avadātavasana*) is also a Buddha. If one does not see one's nature, even one who has shaved off their hair and beard is a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*).

Question: Laypeople have wives and children; since they have not eliminated lustful desire, by what means can they attain Buddhahood? Answer: It is said only that one must see one's nature; it does not say that one must eliminate lustful desire.
It is precisely because one does not see one's nature [that desire persists]. Once one attains the vision of one's nature, lustful desire is fundamentally empty (*śūnya*).
Śānta. From that time forth, [defilements] were severed and eliminated, nor was there any further attachment or clinging. Even if residual habits remained, they could not cause harm. Why?

Because its nature is fundamentally pure (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*). Although it dwells within the physical body of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), its nature is originally pure and cannot be defiled.
The Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is fundamentally without sensation; it has no hunger, no thirst, no cold or heat, no illness, and no [need for] favors.
Affection. There are no kinsmen; there is neither suffering nor pleasure, neither good nor evil, neither long nor short, neither strong nor weak.

Originally, not a single thing exists that can be grasped. It is solely because of clinging to existence that this physical body arises, and with it come the manifestations of hunger, thirst, cold, heat, and pestilential diseases.
If one does not cling, then let things be as they are. If one attains mastery within birth and death, one transforms all things.

The Dharma is shared with the sages; their spiritual powers are sovereign and unimpeded, and there is nowhere they do not abide. If the mind harbors doubt, one must decisively penetrate all realms of experience.
Do not fail to act; it is best to act. Otherwise, one cannot escape the cycle of birth and death.
If one realizes one's nature, even a *caṇḍāla* can attain Buddhahood.
Question: A candāla performs the karma of taking life; how can such a person attain Buddhahood? Answer:

It is said only that one must see one's nature (dharmatā), not that one must perform specific karmic actions. Even if one’s actions differ from others, no karma whatsoever can obstruct [the realization of nature].

Since beginningless, vast kalpas, it is precisely because of not seeing one's nature that one falls into the hells; thus, through the performance of karma, one revolves in the cycle of birth and death. From...
Once you have realized your original nature, you will ultimately cease to engage in karmic actions. If you do not see your nature, even if you recite the Buddha’s name, you cannot avoid retribution;
this is not merely a matter of killing living beings. If you see your nature, doubt is instantly eliminated, and even the act of killing living beings can do nothing to you.

Since the twenty-seventh patriarch in the Western Heaven, there has been only the successive transmission of the mind-seal. My coming now to this land is solely for the purpose of transmitting the Sudden Teaching.

In the Mahāyāna, the mind itself is the Buddha. It does not speak of maintaining precepts, diligent effort, or ascetic practices—even such acts as entering fire or water, climbing upon a wheel of swords, eating once a day, or sitting constantly without lying down—all of these are merely the conditioned dharmas of external paths.

If you recognize the nature of spiritual awakening that underlies all activity and movement, you are then the very mind of all Buddhas; from the Buddhas of the past to those of the future, they have spoken only of transmitting this mind.
There is no other dharma apart from this. If one recognizes this dharma, even an ordinary person who does not recognize a single character is a Buddha.
If one does not recognize the nature of one’s own numinous awareness, then even if one's body were shattered into atoms, one would never find a Buddha.
A Buddha is also called the Dharmakāya, and is also called the Original Mind. This mind has no form or appearance; it has no cause or effect; it has no sinews or bones.
It is like empty space; it cannot be grasped, for it is not of the nature of obstructive matter, nor is it like the views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

This mind can be fully realized by only one person, the Tathāgata; all other sentient beings, being deluded, do not clearly understand it. This mind does not exist apart from the physical body composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*);
if separated from this mind, there would be no capacity for movement, and this body would be insentient, like grass, trees, tiles, or pebbles.

The body is devoid of intrinsic nature. By what cause does it move? If it is the mind itself that moves—whether it be the movement of speech and activity, or seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—all these are the movement and functioning of the mind.
Movement is the movement of the mind; movement is its function. Apart from movement and function there is no mind; apart from the mind there is no movement.
Movement is not the mind, and the mind is not movement. Movement is fundamentally without mind; the mind...
Fundamentally there is no movement. Movement does not depart from the mind; the mind does not depart from movement. There is no movement apart from the mind, and no mind apart from movement.
Movement is the function of the mind; function is the movement of the mind. Movement is precisely the function of the mind; function is precisely the movement of the mind.

Without movement and without function, the essence of function is fundamentally empty. Emptiness is fundamentally without movement. Movement and function are one with the mind; the mind is fundamentally without movement. Therefore, a sutra says: "Moving yet..."

There is no movement. Throughout the day one comes and goes, yet there has never been any going. Throughout the day one sees, yet there has never been any seeing. Throughout the day one laughs, yet there has never been any laughing.
Throughout the day one hears, yet there has never been any hearing. Throughout the day one knows, yet there has never been any knowing.

Throughout the day one rejoices, yet there has never been any rejoicing. Throughout the day one acts, yet there has never been any acting. Throughout the day one abides, yet there has never been any abiding.

Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The path of speech is cut off; the sphere of mental activity ceases. Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are fundamentally and originally perfect stillness (*parinirvāṇa*).
Even anger, joy, pain, and itching—how are they different from a wooden man? It is simply because when one investigates pain and itching, they cannot be found.

Thus the Sūtra says: "Evil karma results in bitter retribution; good karma results in wholesome retribution. Not only does anger lead to falling into hell, but joy [also leads to its own consequences]."
One will then be reborn in heaven. If one knows that the nature of anger and joy is empty, yet does not cling to them, then karma is liberated.

If one does not perceive this nature, there is no basis for lecturing on the sutras; even if one speaks, it will never be exhausted. These points concerning the provisional distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox have been briefly indicated; they cannot be fully detailed here.

The verse says: Mind, mind, mind is difficult to seek. At its broadest, it pervades the Dharma-realm; at its narrowest, not even a needle can pass through. Originally I sought the mind, not the Buddha;
having realized that the three realms are empty and devoid of substance. If you wish to seek the Buddha, simply seek the mind—this very mind itself.
This mind is the Buddha. Originally, when I sought the mind, the mind itself sustained me; seeking the mind, I could not find it, yet I waited for the mind to know itself.
Buddhahood is not obtained from outside the mind; as soon as the mind arises, it is the moment sin arises.
The verse says:
I have come to this land To transmit the Dharma and save those lost in delusion. When the one flower opens into five petals, The fruit will naturally be formed.
The Discourse on the Bloodline of Master Bodhidharma (End)
